reviews.one_line_contribution: A measured upper bound on the query-agnostic memory-curation policy class -- LOO-best fixed configuration, a set-level outcome oracle prune, a GEPA static demonstration search, and a prompted sequential bank editor all land within a few points of volume-matched random selection, while a training-free query-conditional reranker at identical k clears them -- delivered together with the matched-volume random-removal control that the curation literature omits.
reviews.closest_prior_work: Two, and they threaten different halves. (1) arXiv:2603.02473 (retrieval-vs-utilization factorial) is the collider the proposal itself names, and it is correctly handled: it establishes the direction but never measures a ceiling, never replicates seeds, and never fixes injected volume, so the bound survives it. (2) The one the proposal underweights is classical query-conditional selection plus cross-encoder reranking: KATE (Liu et al. 2021) and Rubin et al. (2022) already establish that per-query demonstration retrieval beats a fixed demonstration set, and that a cross-encoder rerank of a bi-encoder top-k beats the bi-encoder ordering is a standard IR result. F6 is billed as the boldest claim in the paper, but as operationalized (C6 = cross-encoder rerank of top-12, inject top-4; C3 = delete 12 of 120 bank items, then bi-encoder top-4) it is a restatement of that IR result rather than a policy-class discovery. The proposal argues the novelty is the magnitude and the oracle-vs-untrained asymmetry; that argument only works if the two arms are matched on retrieval mechanism, and they are not.
reviews.strongest_objection: The Phase-1 centerpiece does not instantiate the policy class the title claims to bound, and the flaw pre-determines both poles of the result. All 8 configurations are rank patterns of size 4 over the BGE retriever's per-query top-12, so every so-called query-agnostic arm has already been conditioned on the query by the retriever before P1 chooses anything; P1 only picks which slice of an already-topically-relevant candidate list to inject. F1 (P1 - P0 <= 2) is therefore close to guaranteed by construction -- eight 4-subsets drawn from the same 12 retrieved items should differ little -- and confirming it says nothing about whether a policy that fixes bank contents before the query, which is exactly what A-MAC, SAGE, and Memory-R1 do, is bounded. The +-2.5 point CI is advertised as making the null informative, but precision on a quantity that is small by design is not evidence for the thesis. Symmetrically, F6's positive pole is confounded: C6 and C3 differ in retrieval mechanism (cross-encoder vs bi-encoder), not only in conditionality, and C3 is further crippled because deleting 12 of 120 items leaves the injected top-4 unchanged for roughly two-thirds of queries, mechanically compressing C1/C2/C3/C9/C10 differences toward the +-3 band that F5 predicts. Both the headline null and the headline positive are thus produced by design choices orthogonal to the claim about decide-before-query policies. A reviewer would write: the paper measures the flatness of the retriever's own top-12 and the well-known benefit of reranking, then reports it as a ceiling on write-time curation.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: (1) Add a genuinely query-agnostic arm to Phase 1: a fixed 4-item package injected for every instance, LOO-best over a pool of item sets with no retriever in the loop. That is the object the write-time literature actually ships, and only its ceiling can be reported as the ceiling on query-agnostic curation; the current rank-pattern P1 should be relabelled as a retrieval-slice ablation. (2) De-confound F6 with a 2x2: bi-encoder vs cross-encoder read-time selection crossed with full bank vs C3-pruned bank. If cross-encoder-on-pruned-bank equals cross-encoder-on-full-bank, that is the clean statement the paper wants; C6 vs C3 as written is not. (3) Sweep prune depth (12 / 36 / 60 / 90 of 120) and report, per Phase-3 condition, the fraction of the 600 instances whose injected top-4 actually changed. Without that number the +-3 nulls in F5 are uninterpretable, because a null under a 10% perturbation is not a null about curation. (4) Replace R2's pooled seed-noise 95th percentile with a per-instance within-instance configuration-label permutation null; seed variance is strongly instance-dependent (boundary instances flip regardless of configuration), so a global threshold will inflate the config-sensitivity fraction and pre-confirm F4. Note also that F4's interaction term is computed as a difference of variance estimates and is a residual bucket, so interaction >= 3x main effect is close to tautological once the main effect is small by design. (5) Raise the GEPA budget or drop the F7 wording: concluding from a 1,200-episode reflective search that the ceiling is a property of the class rather than the search budget invites the obvious rebuttal that the search was underpowered, and the proposal itself names C4 as the most dangerous refuting baseline.
reviews.missing_baseline: A no-memory (k=0) arm in Phase 3. It exists only as a 200-instance Phase-1 reference, yet the track's own prior result is that injecting a retrieved bank fixed zero items and broke six to seven; if C0 through C10 all sit at or below no-memory on the 600 held-out instances, every headline comparison in Phase 3 is a contest among conditions that are jointly worse than doing nothing, and the plan as written cannot detect that. Also omitted: a curation-depth sweep (everything is tested at 12 of 120 removed), a fixed-item static package in Phase 1 as described above, and a cross-encoder-reranked variant of each static condition to separate reranking from pruning in F6.
reviews.preprint_collision: Unusually strong in form and honest in substance -- it names arXiv:2603.02473 as a partial collision, concedes the directional novelty outright rather than arguing around it, states a decidable disagreement (C3 vs C2, P1 vs P0), and retracts a previously load-bearing citation it could not re-verify. I would credit that. But it has specific gaps that the proposal should not be allowed to treat as neutral. First, it never runs a search for the control it claims is universally absent: volume-matched or token-budget-matched deletion controls are most likely to already exist outside agent memory, in RAG context-compression, context-pruning, and lost-in-the-middle work, and the check queries only the memory-curation and read-time-memory neighbourhoods. The claim that no paper reports such a control is therefore under-searched in exactly the region where a collision would hurt most. Second, it reimplements A-MAC (arXiv:2603.04549) as C1 and calls it faithful while admitting it could only retrieve title and venue, not the abstract; a baseline whose method description was never read cannot carry a pre-registered fidelity check, and C1 vs C2 is one of the four conditions declared undroppable. Third, having already had to withdraw MEMAUDIT (arXiv:2605.02199) as unverifiable raises the prior that other IDs in the Related Work (2607.13591, 2606.24428, 2606.06240, 2608.02113) are cited from retrieval snippets rather than read, and the proposal does not say which of its citations it verified beyond metadata. Net: I can name no preprint that already measures this ceiling, so the bound's novelty stands; the direction's novelty is conceded and gone, and F6's novelty is threatened by the pre-2023 conditional-selection and reranking literature rather than by any 2026 preprint.

reviews.one_line_contribution: A pre-registered measurement claiming an upper bound on query-agnostic memory curation: with a frozen bank and injection volume held exactly fixed, the best static policy attainable — LOO-best constant configuration, set-level oracle prune, GEPA search, sequential bank editor — sits within ~2-3 points of random equal-volume selection, while an untrained query-conditional cross-encoder reranker at identical k does not, with a matched-volume random-removal control that separates published curation gains from bank shrinkage.
reviews.closest_prior_work: Two threats, and the proposal only fully absorbs one. (a) arXiv:2603.02473 ("Diagnosing Retrieval vs. Utilization Bottlenecks in LLM Agent Memory") already establishes the direction on a 3x3 write x retrieve factorial; the proposal concedes this and re-centres on the bound, the volume control, and the variance decomposition, which is the right move. (b) The larger and unabsorbed threat is classical query-conditional demonstration selection — KATE (Liu et al. 2021) and Rubin et al. (2022) — combined with datamodel/DemoShapley-style attribution showing near-null marginal per-example effects. Once you accept both, "a constant policy cannot exploit item x query interaction, a retrieval-conditioned one can" is close to analytic rather than empirical. The proposal cites KATE/Rubin and argues the new content is the oracle-strength static side and the zero-supervision conditional side, but that framing only survives if the static arms are genuinely as strong as claimed — see the objection below, where they are not.
reviews.strongest_objection: The design does not measure the class it names, and the two arms carrying the headline are both weaker than advertised. (1) Every 'query-agnostic' arm still runs the BGE retriever at read time: C1/C3/C4/C9/C10 prune the bank and then retrieve top-4, and P0/P1/P2/P3 range over rank patterns defined on the retriever's own top-12. So P1 is not 'the ceiling on any query-agnostic policy' — it is the ceiling over 8 size-4 rank patterns drawn from a single retriever's top-12, a pool engineered to be near-homogeneous. F1 (P1-P0 <= 2) is therefore close to a foregone conclusion and, whatever its CI, it does not license the title's claim about write-time curation. Correspondingly, C6-vs-C3 is not 'conditional beats static at matched information' but 'read-time reranking of top-12 beats bank pruning followed by top-4 retrieval' — a comparison of decision-time information, not of policy class. (2) The C3 'set-level oracle static prune fitted on unlimited probe data' is, by the proposal's own numbers, fitted on ~70 binary observations per item with a stated per-item detectable effect of +-22 points, on a target (the marginal item main effect) that the paper's own thesis predicts is ~0 and that F8 predicts almost no item will clear. An estimator with +-22-point per-item resolution is not an oracle, and the sentence 'a null here cannot be blamed on a weak estimator' is exactly what a reviewer will contest. The claim that the bound is a property of the class 'and not of estimator quality, search budget, or training signal' rests entirely on C3, and C3 cannot bear it. (3) The bank is 400 trajectories distilled by a frontier model and deduped to 120 items — i.e. already curated before the audit begins. Nulls across C1/C3/C9/C10 are then uninterpretable: they are consistent with 'no query-agnostic policy can work' and equally with 'this particular bank has almost no removable harm', and nothing in the design distinguishes them. (4) Power on the headline is razor-thin by the proposal's own arithmetic: F2 predicts P2-P1 >= 5 against an MDE of 4.4, while P2 must learn query-feature interactions from only 199 training queries with a 32-dim query PCA plus per-rank features — branch C is not a tail risk, it is the modal outcome.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: Four changes, in priority order. (1) A positive control with a spiked bank: inject a known set of harmful/contradictory items and verify that C1, C3, C9 and C10 actually remove them and that removal recovers performance. Without a demonstrated detection floor, the whole audit's null is unfalsifiable. (2) Make C3 a real oracle: fit the set-level prune transductively on the Phase-3 instances themselves (in-sample within-pool ceiling), or raise Phase-2 coverage until per-item resolution is comparable to the +-3-point null band. A ceiling claim needs an oracle that is powered on the quantity it optimizes. (3) Widen P1's hypothesis class beyond retriever rank patterns to include content-defined static packages selected independently of the retriever's per-query ordering, so 'query-agnostic' is not smuggling a query-conditional component; and report P1 with the retriever ablated (fixed random top-12 pool) as the true static reference. (4) Add the composition arm — curated bank (C1 or C3) plus the C6 reranker — since the actionable claim ('write-time curation is bounded, spend the budget at read time') requires showing curation adds nothing on top of a good read-time policy, not merely that it loses to one. Also vary bank size/noise (e.g. 120 vs 500 items, deduped vs raw) so the ceiling is reported as a function of bank quality rather than measured once on the most favourable bank for the hypothesis. Separately, the compute arithmetic is wrong by roughly an order of magnitude: at the stated 3,000 tok/s aggregate and ~7,200 generated tokens/episode (8 calls x 900), throughput is ~0.4 episodes/s, not 3, giving ~1,500 episodes/hour before the 3x tool-latency discount and ~500/hour after — 26,200 episodes is ~50 GPU-hours of generation alone, before ~2.5B tokens of prefill, so '7 GPU-hours' and 'under 3 days including a full re-run' should be restated as 1-2 weeks of node time.
reviews.missing_baseline: Two. (a) A positive control / spiked-bank sanity arm establishing that the curation conditions can detect item-level harm at all — its absence makes every static null ambiguous between 'the policy class is bounded' and 'this bank had nothing to prune'. (b) A composition arm: static curation AND read-time conditional selection together (C1+C6, C3+C6) against C6 alone. The paper's recommendation — write-time curation is not worth the budget, fill the demonstration slot at read time — is a claim about complementarity that the plan never tests; write-time and read-time selection are not mutually exclusive in any deployed system. Third, minor but a reviewer will ask: an oracle read-time selector at k=4 over the full 495 size-4 subsets, to show how much of the conditional headroom the 8-pattern pool is hiding on the conditional side too.
reviews.preprint_collision: The check is unusually strong for this genre and should be credited: it names a directional collision (arXiv:2603.02473) rather than hiding it, retracts a prior unverifiable MEMAUDIT anchor, admits it could retrieve only title/venue for the audited target A-MAC (arXiv:2603.04549), reports three search passes, and states the residual risk (a matched-volume random-removal ablation buried in a recent curation appendix) explicitly. I find no preprint that makes the specific bound claim. But two gaps remain. First, the check searches the agent-memory literature and not the adjacent context-compression / selective-RAG literature, where random-drop and random-sentence-removal controls at matched token budget are routine; the claim that matched-volume random removal is 'absent from every curation paper we found' is true only under a narrow reading of 'curation paper', and a reviewer from the compression side will say the control is standard practice being rebranded as a contribution. Second, the check does not search for prior oracle-static-vs-conditional demonstration-selection comparisons in the ICL literature, which is where the proposal's own Related Work section (4) concedes the direction was anticipated by KATE and Rubin et al.; a novelty claim resting on 'the static side is an oracle this time' should have been searched for directly, and was not. Net: the collision check is honest and current, and it correctly reduces the claimed novelty of direction, but it leaves the two searches that most threaten what remains.

reviews.one_line_contribution: A dense factorial + oracle-baseline measurement claiming that the entire class of policies that decide a memory item's fate before the query is known is bounded near random selection at matched injection volume, while an untrained query-conditional reranker (C6) exceeds even an oracle static prune (C3) handed unlimited outcome supervision.
reviews.closest_prior_work: Two threats, in different directions. (1) arXiv:2603.02473 (retrieval-vs-utilization factorial on LoCoMo) already establishes the direction; the proposal concedes this and re-centres on the bound, the volume control, and the variance decomposition, which is the right move and largely works. (2) The more damaging one the proposal treats as settled: KATE (Liu et al., 2021) and Rubin et al. (2022) for query-conditional demonstration retrieval, plus the standard bi-encoder-retrieve/cross-encoder-rerank result from IR. The proposal's headline positive finding (F6: C6 beats C3, C1, C4, C9, C10) is, mechanically, 'a cross-encoder reranker over the top-12 beats a bi-encoder top-4 with 12 of 120 bank items deleted.' That is a known IR result wearing a memory-curation costume; the proposal's own Related Work concedes the direction is anticipated by KATE but then defends the magnitude and the no-supervision framing, neither of which survives if the operative variable is the relevance model rather than conditionality.
reviews.strongest_objection: P1 is not a ceiling on query-agnostic policies, and F1 is close to tautological. All 8 Phase-1 configurations are fixed rank patterns of size 4 drawn from *the retriever's own query-conditional top-12*. A 'constant' choice of rank pattern therefore inherits essentially all of the retriever's query-conditionality; the only thing held query-agnostic is which ranks among 12 already-topically-relevant candidates get used. Finding that no fixed rank pattern beats a random rank pattern by >2 points (F1) says the top-12 are roughly exchangeable in rank order — it says nothing about the audited class, which decides *item identity in the bank*, not rank position at read time. The paper's Risk Factor 3 acknowledges the pool restriction but frames it as a fairness issue ('a richer pool could raise the static ceiling somewhat'); the actual problem is a construct-validity failure, not a power one. Compounding it in Phase 3: C1/C2/C3/C9 all remove 12 items from a 120-item bank from which retrieval injects only 4. For most queries the deleted items were never in the top-4, so the F5 null band (all static conditions within ±3 of random removal) is close to mechanically guaranteed regardless of whether write-time curation carries real signal — and the plan never reports, or controls for, how often removed items would have entered the top-4. A reviewer will read the centrepiece as a bound on rank-pattern selection and the audit as a null manufactured by a 10% prune, and the abstract's claim that 'any published write-time curation gain exceeding the measured static ceiling must come from bank shrinkage' will not be supported by either.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: (1) Add a genuinely query-agnostic arm to Phase 1: a fixed *item-identity* set (the same 4 bank items injected for every query, best-of-pool fitted LOO). The gap between that and the best fixed rank pattern is the actual query-agnostic ceiling, and reporting both separates 'the retriever is doing the work' from 'staticness is bounded'. (2) Break the C6/C3 confound by adding a cross-encoder-matched static arm — e.g. a globally fixed item ordering scored by the same cross-encoder against a query-independent probe, and/or C3+cross-encoder-read as a crossed 2x2 of {static prune, no prune} x {bi-encoder read, cross-encoder read}. Without the crossing, F6 measures reranker quality, not policy class. (3) Sweep the prune fraction (e.g. 10/30/50% of the bank) rather than fixing it at 12/120, and report the rate at which removed items would have appeared in the deployment top-4; a null at a prune depth that barely perturbs retrieval is uninformative. (4) Make the Phase-0 precheck noise-controlled: '≥8% of instances differ in either direction' between memory and no-memory is within the 2.2-6.0 point agentic decoding variance the proposal itself cites, so the gate can pass on noise; require a seed-replicated, paired disagreement rate above the null-replicate band. (5) Either raise Phase-1 to give P2 real training data or drop F2's threshold: a configuration x query-feature interaction model over ~50 features and 8 configurations fitted on 199 instances, with an MDE of 4.4 against a predicted effect of 5, is a coin flip by construction and will most likely land in the pre-declared 'inconclusive' band or in Branch C.
reviews.missing_baseline: A query-agnostic arm that receives the same relevance-model upgrade as C6 — i.e. cross-encoder scoring applied query-independently (a globally fixed cross-encoder-ranked item list, or C3's oracle prune read with the cross-encoder). As written, C6 is the only arm in the paper with a cross-encoder in the read path, so every C6-vs-static comparison in F6 is 'cross-encoder vs BGE' rather than 'conditional vs query-agnostic'. Secondary omissions a reviewer will also demand: a fixed-item-set (same 4 items for all queries) arm in Phase 1, and a no-memory arm in Phase 3 — given this track's own prior finding that memory injection can be one-sidedly harmful, a Phase-3 table in which every curation condition sits within noise of no-memory would reinterpret the entire audit, and the Phase-0 precheck on 150 dev instances does not substitute for it.
reviews.preprint_collision: Well above average and I credit it: it names arXiv:2603.02473 as a partial collision, concedes the directional finding rather than burying it, states a decidable disagreement (C3 vs C2, P1 vs P0), and retracts a prior anchor citation (MEMAUDIT, arXiv:2605.02199) it could not re-verify. Three real gaps remain. First, it admits it could retrieve only title/venue for A-MAC (arXiv:2603.04549), yet the plan pre-registers a 'faithful A-MAC reimplementation' with a specific five-factor score (future utility, factual confidence, semantic novelty, recency, content-type prior) and makes C1-vs-C2 a headline comparison — you cannot pre-commit to fidelity against a paper whose abstract you could not read, and the fidelity check ('reproduce the direction of its published end-to-end effect') is unverifiable against an unretrieved result. Second, the search is entirely on the agent-memory side; there is no recency pass at all on the two literatures where a collision with the *positive* finding is most likely — query-conditional/instance-adaptive demonstration selection post-KATE, and cross-encoder reranking for memory/experience retrieval. Given that F6 is the boldest claim and is exactly a cross-encoder reranking result, the absence of any preprint search in that space is a substantive hole, not a formality. Third, the residual risk it names (a matched-volume random-removal ablation buried in a recent curation preprint's appendix) is real and unresolved, and that control is one of the three things it claims as remaining novelty.
